name: Buddhist Nationalism
summary: Buddhist nationalism holds that the nation's identity is bound up with Theravada Buddhism and that the state must protect the sasana against internal and external threats, chiefly Muslims, Christian missions and, in Sri Lanka, Tamil separatism. Its programmes call for state primacy for Buddhism, restrictions on conversion and interfaith marriage, a unitary state, and economic and cultural defence of the majority, with Muslim minorities as the main target. It says little on economics, welfare or most other policy questions.
scope: The national position only: the Sinhala Buddhist strand in Sri Lanka (Mahavamsa tradition, Anagarika Dharmapala, Jathika Hela Urumaya, Bodu Bala Sena, Sinhala Ravaya) and the Burmese strand (969 movement, MaBaTha). Positions on the economy, welfare, taxation and similar matters are null because the sources record none that the nationalists state as part of the national cause; the programmes of the governments and parties that carried it are not used. Excludes Thai royalist nationalism and Buddhist modernists who reject nationalism.

sources.title: Jathika Hela Urumaya and Ethno-Religious Politics in Sri Lanka (abstract)
sources.author: Neil DeVotta and Jason Stone, Pacific Affairs 81(1), 2008
sources.usedFor: Only the abstract was open: the JHU's goals and policies resemble those of other Buddhist nationalist groups.

more-religion-public.rationale: The Jathika Hela Urumaya's general secretary states the party's main policy is a unitary Buddhist state ruled according to the Buddha's doctrines, and Walton and Hayward describe the movements as making Buddhism the state's primary moral touchstone.

separate-church-state.rationale: The JHU's stated aim is a Buddhist state governed by the Buddha's doctrines, and Walton and Hayward note that where the sasana is thought threatened these movements let democracy revert to theocracy.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The JHU says the country will be ruled by the doctrines of the Buddha, and the Sinhala Ravaya group (also Sinhala Buddhist nationalist) demanded a constitution founded on Buddhist law; the Buddha's teachings are the canon, not a lawcode, hence medium.

national-church-status.rationale: The JHU's first stated policy is a unitary Buddhist state, and the Burmese movements campaigned for the sasana's protection by the state, building on the 1961 State Religion Promotion Act that U Nu championed (never in force) according to ICG.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The JHU promised to bring in a bill against unethical conversions at once, and MaBaTha and 969 lobbied for Myanmar's Religious Conversion Law (2015), which makes conversion subject to a township board's permission.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Monks of 969 and MaBaTha collected signatures for and lobbied for the Buddhist Women's Special Marriage Law, enacted August 2015, which puts any marriage of a Buddhist woman to a non-Buddhist man under a public registrar procedure.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The 969 movement's 'Buy Buddhist' campaign urged Buddhists to patronise only Buddhist-owned shops, which Wirathu defended as protecting his people's interests; the BBS ran an anti-halal campaign against Muslim-certified goods.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Wirathu and Ashin Sada Ma preached a Muslim conspiracy to take over Myanmar through money, marriage and conversion, and the BBS claimed Middle Eastern funds were converting Sri Lankan Buddhists.

religious-nation.rationale: MaBaTha's very name ties race (a-myo), religion (batha) and the sasana together, and the JHU defines the country as a Buddhist state; Walton and Hayward describe national identity as bound up in Buddhism.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Protecting the nation's Buddhist culture is the stated purpose of 969, MaBaTha ('protection of race and religion'), the BBS and the JHU, and Dharmapala's revival campaign aimed at the same end.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: 969's Buy Buddhist campaign and Wirathu's warnings of Muslim economic takeover, the BBS's claim that pluralism robbed Sinhalese of money and enterprise, and Dharmapala's call to end dependence on immigrant Muslim traders all aim at majority control of commerce.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: MaBaTha and associated monks developed Buddhist religious education programmes for public schools besides their Sunday schools, so the movement wants religious instruction in state schools.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: A state bound to protect and foster the Buddha sasana, as the JHU and MaBaTha demand, cannot also promote atheism through its schools.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The JHU is a party of Buddhist monks that campaigns for a Bauddha Rajjya, and MaBaTha lobbied electorally on race-and-religion laws, so organising politics around a religion is their method; MaBaTha itself was loosely non-party, hence medium.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: BBS general secretary Gnanasara told the 2013 Maharagama rally that a country must have a single legal system applying to all ethnic and religious groups, aimed at Muslim personal law; Myanmar's monogamy law was likewise championed as binding all communities.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The BBS demanded one legal system for all and campaigned to end halal certification and Muslim dress, rejecting carve-outs for a minority's religious practice.

decide-locally.rationale: Stated by the Sinhala Buddhist strand only; the Burmese strand is not shown to share it.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Stated by the Sinhala Buddhist strand only; the Burmese strand is not shown to share it.

right-to-secede.rationale: Stated by the Sinhala Buddhist strand only; the Burmese strand is not shown to share it.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Stated by the Sinhala Buddhist strand only; the Burmese strand is not shown to share it.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Walton and Hayward report that Sri Lankan monks defend the integrity of the island as a Buddhist homeland and that Wirathu says the movement protects the country as well as the sasana; the Mahavamsa makes the island the guardian of the doctrine.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The JHU wants the economy and the state both governed by Dhamma values, and Dharmapala saw religious revival, moral uplift and economic development as one movement.

political-violence-never.rationale: Official statements of 969 and MaBaTha disavow violence, yet scholars report just-war rhetoric defending violence for the sasana and the Mahavamsa's Dutthagamani story treats killing unbelievers as no grave matter; Dharmapala stayed nonviolent. Strands differ.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The JHU says all races and religions will enjoy rights in a Buddhist state, but the Mahavamsa has the arahants call slain unbelievers no more to be esteemed than beasts, and Wirathu and the BBS demand curbs on Muslims; the sources point both ways.

missingStatements.text: Monks should take part directly in party politics and government.
missingStatements.rationale: The JHU, a party composed of Buddhist monks, was founded to take the Maha Sangha into parliament, and Walton and Hayward say 969 and MaBaTha justify monastic political action as a duty to protect the sasana.

missingStatements.text: Foreign funding for building mosques and for religious conversion should be banned.
missingStatements.rationale: The BBS's Maharagama Declaration called for a ban on mosque-building with Middle Eastern funds, and its leaders alleged foreign funds were converting Buddhists.

notes: Themes searched: government, society, liberty, world, culture, means, economy, globalism. Economic, welfare, ecology and technology positions are null because no source states them as part of the national cause. Several answers (decide-locally, minority-territorial-autonomy, right-to-secede) rest on Sri Lankan sources only; Burmese sources are silent. Walton and Hayward note MaBaTha was a loose coalition and that its leaders formally deny advocating violence.
